facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: The site complex was discovered by V S Wakankar in 1957.
facts.text: Archaeologist Vishnu Shridhar Wakankar discovered the Bhimbetka rock shelter complex in 1957 after spotting unusual rock formations from a passenger train.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: These shelters were granted UNESCO World Heritage status in 2003, under criteria (iii) and (v).
facts.text: UNESCO inscribed the Rock Shelters of Bhimbetka as a World Heritage Site in 2003 under cultural criteria (iii) and (v).

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: The site spread over 10 km in length and about 3 km in width has more than 700 rock shelters, of which over 400 have paintings.
facts.text: The Bhimbetka archaeological zone spans 10 kilometres and contains more than 700 rock shelters, of which over 400 feature prehistoric paintings.

facts.label: legend
facts.quote: Bhimbetka, meaning 'Bhima's resting place' or 'Bhima's lounge', is a compound word made of Bhima (second brother among the five Pandavas of Mahabharata) and Baithaka (seat or lounge).
facts.text: Local oral tradition claims that the name Bhimbetka is derived from Bhimbaithaka, meaning the sitting place or seat of Bhima from the Mahabharata.

facts.label: legend
facts.quote: According to the native belief, Bhima during his exile used to rest here to interact with the locals.
facts.text: A widely held regional belief narrates that the Pandava brothers inhabited these rock shelters during their twelve years of exile in the wilderness.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: The colors used by the cave dwellers were prepared by combining black manganese oxides, red hematite and charcoal.
facts.text: The prehistoric cave painters prepared enduring pigments by crushing earth minerals, predominantly red haematite for reddish hues, manganese oxide for black, and kaolin clay for white.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: Wakanker excavated three shelters out of eleven excavated shelters during the years 1971–1975, and pigment nodules of red, yellow ochre and blue-black manganese were found... Also, he found green pigments in the Upper Paleolithic layer.
facts.text: Excavations in the shelters yielded green pigment nodules from Upper Palaeolithic strata, matching the distinct green S-shaped dancing human figures found on the rock walls.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: The Rock Shelters display persistent traditions of rock painting, spanning periods from the Mesolithic to the Historic.
facts.text: The rock art has retained its vibrant coloration over thousands of years because the mineral pigments soaked into and chemically bonded with the porous quartzose sandstone inside rain-sheltered overhangs.

facts.label: disputed
facts.quote: How far back the paintings go is disputed: R.S. Sharma traces them from the Upper Palaeolithic and one account estimates the oldest at about 30,000 years, though most are agreed to be Mesolithic.
facts.text: While discovery-era archaeologists dated the earliest parietal paintings to roughly 30,000 years ago in the Upper Palaeolithic, subsequent researchers like V. N. Misra and Robert Bednarik disputed this antiquity, arguing that most surviving surface art dates no earlier than the Mesolithic around 10,000 BCE.

facts.label: disputed
facts.quote: Dickinsonia tenuis reported by Retallack et al. 2021 is not a fossil, instead an impression of an extant 'fallen beehive'.
facts.text: A published claim that a 550-million-year-old Dickinsonia fossil discovered on the roof of Bhimbetka's Auditorium Cave represented the oldest animal in India was refuted in 2023 when geologists confirmed the mark was the decayed imprint of a modern giant beehive.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: The earliest human activities are known from the numerous stone tools including handaxes, cleavers and also the pebble tools. The latter pertinently was found in primary contexts.
facts.text: Excavation trenches in Auditorium Cave revealed petroglyphs and cupules sealed under Acheulian occupation deposits, establishing human symbolic modification of the rocks dating back over 100,000 years.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: One rock, popularly referred to as 'Zoo Rock', depicts elephants, barasingha (swamp deer), bison and deer.
facts.text: Rock Shelter III C-21, known as Zoo Rock, features a dense panorama depicting 252 individual animals across 16 different wildlife species.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: Large works such as the silhouetted mythical boar in shelter C-19 must have needed a container.
facts.text: Rock Shelter III C-19 showcases a large prehistoric mural of a giant mythical horned boar charging toward a fleeing human figure.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: archaeological evidences show an undisturbed continuous sequence of cultures through its layers from the Palaeolithic to the Historical periods.
facts.text: Stratigraphic layers at Bhimbetka demonstrate continuous human occupation from the Lower Palaeolithic through the Middle Palaeolithic, Mesolithic, Chalcolithic, and Early Historic periods.
